st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account of jagged capability and human oversight by showing that perceived AI authority can reshape user reasoning even without genuine predictive capability, persist after repeated failures, and create self-reinforcing apparent performance. This adds a psychological and interaction-design mechanism for over-reliance, while its controlled non-legal setting limits direct inference about legal workflows.
qs: In our experiments, the AI systems did not perform any algorithmic prediction and so the observed effects reflect human psychology alone.

Addressing the societal impact of AI will therefore require attention not only to what AI predicts or does, but also to how the perceived authority of AI reshapes the decisions people experience as their own.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between apparent AI performance and measured underlying capability. Its repeated-interaction experiment shows that users’ behavioral adaptation can increase observed predictive accuracy even when the AI’s prediction policy is unchanged, while not establishing workplace productivity effects.
qs: (B) This behavioral adaptation altered apparent AI accuracy over time.

Accuracy increased when the AI consistently predicted two-boxing, while remaining relatively stable when it consistently predicted one-boxing, resulting in a significant increase in overall accuracy (slope 𝑝 = 0.002) despite the prediction policy remaining fixed throughout the study.

kp.k: Predictive authority changes decisions without revealing predictions
kp.d: This cross-domain behavioral study examines human decision-making, not legal services. Four preregistered online studies involved 1,305 unique participants recruited through Prolific. In an adaptation of Newcomb’s paradox, Box A guaranteed US$1 and Box B contained US$0 or US$3, determined before participants chose either both boxes or Box B alone. Participants were told an AI had predicted their choice, but neither its prediction nor its reliability was disclosed. The authors argue that perceived predictive authority can change reasoning about future actions without recommending a particular choice.
qs: The system neither revealed its prediction nor provided any recommendation at the time of choice, ruling out explicit AI persuasion
At the time of choice, participants are, however, not told the prediction or what Box B contains.

kp.k: AI framing increased forgoing guaranteed rewards
kp.d: Study 1, conducted in February 2025 with 200 participants, found one-boxing among 41.0% in the AI condition versus 26.0% in the random condition (p = 0.025). Study 2, conducted from December 2025 to January 2026 with 601 participants, found one-boxing rates of 45.0% for non-interactive AI and 42.0% for interactive AI, versus 15.3% in both random conditions. A fixed-effect meta-analysis of Studies 1 and 2 reported an odds ratio of 3.39 (95% CI: 2.45–4.70; p < 0.001). The reported 10.7–42.9% earnings reduction is relative to a two-boxing baseline and depends on the prediction regime; the supplementary analysis calculates bounds for always-one-box and always-two-box predictions.
qs: In the AI condition, 41 of 100 participants (41.0%) chose one-boxing, compared with 26 of 100 (26.0%) in the random condition
In contrast, one-boxing was substantially more frequent when decisions were framed as predicted by AI (45.0% in the non-interactive AI condition and 42.0% in the interactive AI condition).

The lower bound corresponds to a prediction regime in which the AI always predicts one-boxing (yielding payoffs of 3 or 4), whereas the upper bound corresponds to a regime in which the AI always predicts two-boxing (yielding payoffs of 0 or 1).

kp.k: Conversational interaction did not significantly strengthen the effect
kp.d: Study 2 varied predictor identity and prior interaction. Interactive AI participants completed eight conversational exchanges using GPT-4.1, while non-interactive participants received an AI label without system-specific interaction. One-boxing did not differ significantly between interactive and non-interactive conditions: the reported Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise p-values were 1.000 for both predictor types. The authors interpret the comparable effects across a virtual agent, an LLM assistant and an AI label as evidence that perceived authority matters more than technical sophistication in this setting.
qs: Non-interactive conditions removed all system-specific interaction and described the outcome as determined by either an “AI system” or a “random generator.”
The chatbot was implemented using the OpenAI GPT-4.1 API (model version: gpt-4.1-2025-04-14).
The chatbot conducted exactly eight conversational turns before concluding the interaction.

kp.k: Human experts produced stronger effects than AI
kp.d: Study 3, conducted in March 2026 with 303 participants, tested hypothetical job-interview, mobile-data-coupon and freelancing-task decisions. One-box-type choices occurred in 26.7% of cases under AI prediction, 36.6% under human-expert prediction and 10.6% without prediction. AI differed significantly from control (p < 0.001), while human prediction produced a larger effect than AI (odds ratio = 1.67, p = 0.032). These are vignette choices, not observed employment or purchasing outcomes. The findings support a broader predictive-authority mechanism rather than an exclusively AI-specific effect.
qs: Across scenarios, participants chose the one-box option in 26.7% of the cases under AI prediction and 36.6% under human-expert prediction, compared to 10.6% without prediction
Human-expert predictions produced a somewhat larger effect than AI predictions (odds ratio = 1.67, 𝑝 = 0.032).
While the direction of the effect was consistent across scenarios, its magnitude varied

kp.k: Perceived accuracy alone did not explain choices
kp.d: In Study 2, participants attributed above-chance accuracy to AI despite receiving no reliability information: 62.1% for non-interactive AI and 62.9% for interactive AI, both p < 0.001. Random-system estimates were approximately chance-level at 50.4% and 49.7%. However, one-boxers and two-boxers did not differ significantly in perceived AI accuracy (p = 0.080 and p = 0.634). The authors therefore propose that perceived predictiveness must be considered alongside internal coherence—the tendency to act consistently with anticipated actions. Beliefs were collected after choice but before outcome disclosure.
qs: Notably, they formed these beliefs despite receiving no information about the system’s ostensible predictive accuracy.
Perceived predictiveness alone, however, was insufficient to explain one-boxing.
Individuals who believe that their anticipated action has been predicted may nevertheless choose two-boxing if they treat their actual action as independent of the prediction.

kp.k: Reasoning mechanism remains suggestive rather than decisively established
kp.d: The proposed mechanism contrasts causal reasoning, under which taking both boxes adds a guaranteed US$1, with evidential reasoning, under which actions are treated as evidence of a prior prediction. A mixture model fit Study 2 better than random-choice, causal-only or evidential-only models. Internal coherence was estimated at condition level, not directly measured for each participant. Its posterior mean was 0.682 for AI and 0.443 for random conditions, but the posterior probability that the AI parameter exceeded the random parameter was only 82.6%, below the authors’ example 95% threshold. The supplementary analysis explicitly qualifies the claim that AI shifts reasoning.
qs: In the model, greater internal coherence corresponds to a higher probability of evaluating the task through evidential rather than causal reasoning.
However, the posterior probability that 𝑞 𝐴𝐼 > 𝑞𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑜𝑚 was 82.6%, which does not reach a conventional evidential threshold (e.g., 95%).
although the present data do not provide decisive statistical evidence for this difference.

kp.k: Higher AI literacy did not prevent one-boxing
kp.d: Exploratory analyses linked one-boxing to higher AI literacy, encompassing awareness, usage and evaluation (p = 0.011), and greater risk-taking preference (p = 0.003). The authors report no association with sociodemographic variables, beliefs about free will or determinism, or affective attitudes toward AI. They interpret this pattern as inconsistent with attributing the effect simply to limited understanding of AI. These are associations, not experimental effects of literacy or risk preference.
qs: Sociodemographic variables and beliefs about free will or determinism, as well as affective attitudes toward AI, showed no association with choice in the task.
This pattern is inconsistent with explanations attributing the effect to limited understanding of AI.

kp.k: Behavioral adaptation increased apparent accuracy without model improvement
kp.d: Study 4, conducted in January 2026 with 201 participants, used five rounds and fixed prediction policies. One-boxing remained stable when AI always predicted one-boxing (slope p = 0.763), but declined when it always predicted two-boxing (slope p < 0.001; interaction p = 0.002). Overall prediction accuracy increased from 50.7% to 59.2% (slope p = 0.002), although the policy never changed. Average perceived accuracy remained approximately 57.6%, with no significant overall time trend (p = 0.513). The authors interpret this as consistent with a self-fulfilling prophecy: people adapt, making a fixed predictor appear more capable.
qs: Participants were not informed of the prediction policy, and the system did not update its predictions during the task.
Accuracy significantly increased when the AI consistently predicted two-boxing, while remaining relatively stable when the AI consistently predicted one-boxing.
Ongoing interactions around AI predictions may therefore make AI appear increasingly capable, even in the absence of computational improvements.

kp.k: Repeated failures did not eliminate the behavioral effect
kp.d: In Study 4’s always-two-box prediction condition, final-round one-boxing remained at 30.6%, compared with 15.3% in Study 2’s random conditions (p = 0.003). The authors interpret persistence despite repeated predictive mismatches as evidence that AI can continue influencing reasoning after failures. The comparison is with a separate study’s baseline: Study 4 did not include a concurrent random-generator condition.
qs: These results indicate that AI
prediction can influence people’s reasoning and behavior even when they experience its repeated failures.
we did not include a random-generator condition.

kp.k: Agency implications extend beyond irrationality claims
kp.d: The authors explicitly decline to characterize one-boxing as inherently irrational: it can be rational under evidential expected-utility reasoning. Their interpretation is that predictive authority binds anticipated actions to predicted futures, restricting which alternatives people regard as plausible despite their objective freedom to choose. Broader implications for cooperation, collective action and human agency are proposed extensions, not directly tested outcomes of these experiments.
qs: We do not interpret this pattern as irrationality per se.
That is, predictive authority binds people’s anticipated actions to what the system predicts, narrowing the futures they themselves regard as plausible.
In this sense, AI could either support or undermine human cooperation, depending on which behaviors become anticipated and reinforced within a given environment

kp.k: Controlled psychology findings do not establish real-world predictive effects
kp.d: The authors emphasize that the experimental AI systems performed no algorithmic prediction; the findings concern psychological responses to perceived authority. The minimal setting omitted strategic interaction, social norms, and cultural and historical context. The possibility that genuinely accurate systems could create stronger or more persistent effects is a future-facing hypothesis. The supplied arXiv version is dated 3 July 2026, and the document states that data will become available upon publication.
qs: In our experiments, the AI systems did not perform any algorithmic prediction and so the observed effects reflect human psychology alone.
This design necessarily omits many features of real-world choice, including strategic interaction, social norms, and cultural and historical context
Real-world AI systems with verifiable predictive accuracy may elicit stronger or more persistent beliefs, potentially amplifying the effects observed here.
The data generated and analyzed will be available upon publication.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Naito and Shirado claim that perceived AI predictive authority can change decision-making itself, narrowing the futures people consider and producing self-reinforcing behavioral adaptation.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about human decision-making, not legal services. The authors report that framing a predetermined outcome as an AI prediction increased participants’ likelihood of forgoing a guaranteed reward. They interpret this as people linking their anticipated actions to what they believe the system has predicted, rather than treating their available actions as independent of the prediction. Across Studies 1 and 2, they report a pooled odds ratio of 3.39 (95% CI: 2.45–4.70) for forgoing the guaranteed reward. They report earnings reductions of 10.7–42.9% relative to a two-boxing baseline, with the supplementary analysis specifying bounds under alternative fixed prediction regimes. In repeated interaction, apparent prediction accuracy increased through changes in human behavior rather than improvements to the system. Their broader predictions are that AI could become a source of predictive authority and could support or undermine cooperation depending on the behaviors reinforced. These societal implications are proposed extensions, not outcomes directly established by the experiments.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of four preregistered online experiments with 1,305 unique participants, supplemented by self-reports, qualitative responses and computational modeling.
pts.d: Study 1 (N = 200) found one-boxing in 41.0% of the AI condition versus 26.0% of the random condition (p = 0.025). Study 2 (N = 601) found 45.0% and 42.0% one-boxing in non-interactive and interactive AI conditions, respectively, versus 15.3% in both random conditions; system interaction did not significantly moderate the effect. Study 3 (N = 303) used hypothetical job-interview, mobile-data and freelancing scenarios: one-box-type choices occurred in 26.7% of AI cases, 36.6% of human-expert cases and 10.6% of no-prediction cases. Study 4 (N = 201) used five rounds with fixed prediction policies; overall prediction-choice agreement rose from 50.7% to 59.2%. The authors report that final-round one-boxing in the two-box-prediction condition remained at 30.6%, above Study 2’s random baseline of 15.3%; that comparison uses a separate study rather than a concurrent repeated-round random control. Study 2 accuracy beliefs averaged 62.1–62.9% for AI despite no supplied reliability information. A mixture of causal and evidential reasoning fit best among the tested computational models, but the supplementary analysis expressly says the estimated AI-versus-random difference in internal coherence was not statistically decisive: posterior probability 82.6%, below the cited 95% threshold. Internal coherence was estimated at condition level, not measured independently for each participant. The authors’ societal predictions draw on these findings and theoretical literature rather than field evidence of collective outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern immediate choices and five-round interactions in experiments conducted in 2025–2026; longer-term and real-world effects remain prospective.
pts.d: Study 1 took place in February 2025, Study 2 from December 2025 to January 2026, Study 4 in January 2026, and Study 3 in March 2026. In the monetary task, Box A guaranteed US$1 and Box B contained US$0 or US$3; participants were told that Box B’s contents were already fixed, and the prediction was not revealed until after choice. The systems did not actually algorithmically predict behavior. Comparable effects appeared with a virtual agent, an LLM-based assistant and an AI label alone. The authors qualify their reasoning account: perceived predictiveness alone was insufficient, and they do not describe one-boxing as necessarily irrational under evidential reasoning. Repeated-interaction findings cover only five rounds. The authors acknowledge that the minimal design excludes strategic interactions, social norms and cultural or historical context. Stronger or more persistent effects from genuinely accurate predictive systems are possibilities for future investigation, with no specified forecast horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is adult online participants; the proposed wider relevance is to people interacting with predictive systems and to collective human–machine settings.
pts.d: Participants were adults recruited through Prolific without regional restrictions and with a minimum platform approval rate of 95%. The observed effects concern their reward choices, earnings, reasoning and adaptation to feedback. Vignettes represent job seekers, mobile-phone customers and freelance-platform workers, but do not establish effects on actual employment, consumer or platform outcomes. The authors suggest that predictive authority may shape the agency people experience and the expectations governing cooperation. They also suggest that observers may mistake behavior-driven increases in prediction accuracy for improved AI capability. Human experts produced a larger effect than AI in Study 3, so the proposed influence is not unique to AI. No findings are presented about lawyers, law firms, legal buyers or legal markets.
